title: Why he plays Albert system, and buying a Selmer
summary: Hall explains his preference for the Albert system's bigger low-register tone and tells of visiting the Selmer factory in France.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: The Albert system. I mean, judging mostly from Grant Card.
Yeah. Some of my friends, they all, the clarinetists we like, they all play Albert system, so it looks like they must be better. It's about everything.

I'll tell you another story. I went to Old Man Selma when I bought that instrument. And a lot of people come up and ask me, they say, well, why you play Albert system? I say, well, when I started playing, it wasn't making no BEM system. You say, well, how long they been making BEM system? I say, well, I remember seeing my first BEM run about, about 30 years ago. So when they'd asked me how long BEM was made, I say, oh, about 30 years ago. So what happens when I go to this factory, so I'm buying a, buying a Selma Klein. So I, this guy, he's a, what's his name, Old Man Selma, but his son got the factory. So I said, tell me something. I want to ask you a question. I said, how long BEM was made? He said, because they don't make Albert system anymore. So he said, oh, but by the way, I have the first one that was made. So he goes in the show window and pull out the first BEM was made. His father made it, father played it. And he mentioned after the Germans heard about it, the, the, the system. And it was made in 18, 18, 18, what? 1853. Over a hundred years ago. You remember my toilet paper?
